588.t: Mother leaves the farm for Kalamazoo and segregated high school
588.s: After the separation her mother moved the family to Kalamazoo, where Abbey attended the hilltop high school while living in servants' quarters.
588.q: When my mother left my father, she brought the kids to Kalamazoo. She brought us to Kalamazoo after awhile because it really wasn't her setting. It wasn't ours either. We weren't farmers and she finally gave it up.

588.t: Making her own clothes and wearing her hair as a teenager
588.s: She sewed outfits from scraps, wore riding boots and ribbons, and became notorious for her style while being told her hair was no good.
588.q: Mm-hmm. The sewing machine was the kind that you did with your feet, and I remember by the time I was 18, the last year I was graduating -- well, it had become a style in school for -- Jane Leander was a beautiful queen at the school. Her father was a lawyer and she was blond with blue eyes and she…

93.t: Practising J. D.'s steps with bottle tops at Five Points
93.s: Back to the bottle caps, he practises the steps J. D. gave him on the streets of Five Points and draws curious crowds.
93.q: That's all they showed, you know? I mean, you see, moving pictures was white, you know, but that's what happened, you see, by -- so far as the bottle tops are concerned, I mean, whatever my partner, Chuckles J. D., used to teach me, steps or something, I would -- after school I would go up

93.t: Skipping kindergarten recess for the Palmetto swimming hole
93.s: Asked where he learned it, Green tells of leaving school grounds with other children on his first kindergarten day for the Palmetto swimming hole in Georgia.
93.ch: Split, hospital and decline of tap
93.q: to pay a debt back, you see. My life got saved accidentally, you know. I almost got adopted by the 13th wonder of the world, which is Jumbo the Elephant. I thought it was an out house -- I didn't know, you see.

430.t: Banging on chairs as a kid and street-corner groups
430.s: As a boy he drummed with chair sticks while friends whistled on street corners, chased off by mounted police; Dave DePas and Yank Johnson come up.
430.q: No, I used to, I was the main attraction. I was always the main attraction. And the guys would have maybe a comb and they'd whistle. And I'd play the drums. At that time I got two sticks from the chairs, from the old chair, and I made the points on them, you know, playing out. What kind of whistle?…

121.t: Childhood games, sports and renting bicycles
121.s: Baseball and tackle football on the green, hopscotch, cowboys and Indians, and shining shoes for bicycle money.
121.q: Oh, yeah, well, the games that we played, not the Spokin games, just the other games. Yeah. Oh, well, football. I played baseball, football. But I was never really good in basketball. But I was a pretty good baseball player. And I could run. I always could run by.

404.t: Neighborhood life and Mitchell as scout leader
404.s: Harold on the neighborhood where everyone belonged to clubs; Mitchell on his Boy Scouts group and how children's respect has faded.
404.ch: Safe streets, decline and club life at San Jacinto
404.q: Boy scout. Oh, that's the same thing. Yeah. Because I had a group over there. Mm-hmm. Boy, I tell you, we had everything, everything you could mention. Everything. Yeah, it seemed like I got, that wouldn't be happening.

667.t: Settling in Las Vegas and the kids in school
667.s: Buying a house and working the gambling circuit while the children attend school.
667.q: And it was really nice living there too, because even though it was Las Vegas, it wasn’t like it is now, it was just like a little sleepy town except for the Strip. The Strip had all the big casinos and everything, and that was kind of bright and wonderful and a lot of great people were coming into…

985.t: The barber shop as a place of learning
985.s: As the youngest he sat in the barber shop for hours, swept hair, ran for food, and learned to take a little from everyone.
985.ch: The barber shop and Uncle's saxophone
985.q: I mean that was, for me that was the place where I learned most things. You know, the time I would go to the barber shop, and for us, since I was the young one, I was the youngest, my brother would drop me off at the barber shop and if there were ten people in front of me and then he would come…

101.t: Boyhood sports and boxing lessons with Kid Carter
101.s: Hurdles, broad jump and dash, and a neighbourhood former champion who taught the kids boxing.
101.q: Kid Carter was the gentleman in the neighborhood who used to gather up all of us kids and teach us the manly art of self defense. He taught it to us the hard way. He’d walked up to you and punch you in the belly. Bam. “Get that – suck that belly in. Tighten up them muscles.” He gave us all a very…

108.s: A stone in a jacket and a chalk mishap get him blamed at school.
108.q: The stones you have in the window reminded me of something that happened when I was in elementary school in Philadelphia. I used to collect round stones like that.

111.t: Pontiac's size and joining the Boy Scouts
111.s: He gives the town's population and describes a World War I veteran scoutmaster who taught discipline.
111.q: It was about 60,000. It was quite—that’s a good number of people. But everybody lived in houses so it looked a lot more dense than it really was cause most people they had some pretty big families. Like I said, the people across the street from me.

492.t: Swimming, ping-pong and Ornette's oatmeal cookies
492.s: Lloyd talks about being a Memphis diving champion, ping-pong at the YMCA, and Ornette and he sharing cheese and cookies while playing.
492.ch: Higgins, Hendrix and the spiritual path
492.q: I was a swimmer, I was a junior Olympic swimming champion. My wife’s ­ Dorothy’s - Oh. I wasn’t a junior Olympic swimmer. She was a junior Olympic swimming champ! That’s why you can’t give yourself roses.

228.t: Summers in Greensboro: cowboy movies and games with cousins
228.s: Saturday cowboy films in the black theater, rolling tires, slingshots and errands on his bike.
228.ch: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
228.q: It was cowboys against cowboys a lot of times too. But it’s always the guy with the big white hat and the white horse that always won. Lash LaRue. Some of those guys’ names I can still remember. Then of course, after we saw the movie, then we would come home, playing the movie, running along the…

229.t: His father's upbringing and Blakeney's schooling
229.s: His father was raised by a white family and became a teacher; Blakeney starts school in 1903 and quits after the seventh or eighth grade.
229.q: My father was born in Quitman, Mississippi, November 29, 1864. The year before the surrender he always told it. He was the youngest of seven. At four years old his mother passed, not knowing who or what his father was; a white family took him in in their home.

145.t: Boyhood chores and community values compared with today
145.s: Royal contrasts neighborhood discipline and working for everything with the looser upbringing of today's children.
145.ch: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
145.q: We -- when I was a kid, I always liked to get out and see what was happening with the other kids around the neighborhood. I never really had a paper route of my own or we called them routes in those days, routes probably, but we called them paper routes. I'd get up at 3:00 in the morning just to be…

166.t: Boy Scout troop as a cover to go to a party with his cousin
166.s: He used scouting weekends as an excuse to get out and attend a party with his cousin.
166.q: No, this was Sharpie. (Laughter). So he says all right after he had made his rounds. He says for Friday night, he says can you get out of the house. I says sure, I can get out of the house. He says well I'm ping to take you to a party with me. Well now my excuse to get out of the house on Friday…

28.t: Kindergarten at Hardicht's Brewery, learning German, the ice house
28.s: His mother worked at a German brewery whose kindergarten taught the children German; they pasted labels on bottles and played dangerously in the ice house.
28.q: then my mother's moved back to E Street, right across from the school, and I started school and learning was something I had to have. I knew I had to have it. I had to have knowledge. I knew that. So I went to kindergarten and kindergarten was nothing for me. I was making rabbits and horses and…

236.t: Ice skating as a boy and on the road
236.s: He tells of boyhood skating and of skating with the band behind a gymnasium.
236.q: : Jesus... I used to skate like crazy all winter, you know. And I graduated from regular skates to box-toes to racers, and I had 18-inch racers. And I could really handle 'em. There was a pond about a half to three-quarters of a mile from my house that used to freeze over every winter, and we used…
